item.title: Sariling Kuryente Act Promises “Own Electricity” While Filipinos Still Pay for Imported Fuel: [Op-Ed]
item.dc:creator: Eileen Lui
item.description: The Philippines has streamlined permits for rooftop solar, but upfront costs of PHP 150,000–350,000 still put it out of reach for most households, and the House bills under consideration offer financing access without subsidies or tax relief for those who can't borrow. Congress should follow Thailand's model by writing both financing and subsidies into the final Sariling Kuryente Act, preserving the VAT exemption on panels, and funding micro solar kits for low-income families. item.title: COP31 ends without a deal. What does it mean for Asia’s energy transition?
item.dc:creator: Wendy Lo
item.description:
Despite the failure of global climate negotiations at COP31, Asia’s electrification push is gaining momentum. However, concerns persist over carbon capture and climate finance.

item.title: Extending energy crisis policies would cut fuel import bills, IEA says
item.dc:creator: Wendy Lo
item.description:
The IEA says Southeast Asia could cut its fossil fuel import bill by more than 20% by 2035 by making its Hormuz policy responses permanent. Grid investment and affordable financing remain key to realizing these gains.

The post Extending energy crisis policies would cut fuel import bills, IEA says appeared first on Energy Tracker Asia.

item.title: As COP31 talks AI, Asia highlights power demand uncertainty
item.dc:creator: Wendy Lo
item.description:
As COP31 puts AI’s energy footprint in focus, Southeast Asia faces uncertainty over future data center electricity demand. A new study examines how renewable energy and regional grid interconnections could help meet that demand.
